title: Charlie's Angels: Full Throttle
full_review:
Like uncorking a bottle of champagne and letting the bubbles tickle one's nose, "Charlie's Angels: Full Throttle" (Columbia) is an effervescent, giddy ride that duplicates the first, which isn't necessarily a bad thing.

Inspired by the popular 1970s' TV show and again directed by McG, the sequel is more of the same slick action scenes with empowered women in heels drop.kicking the bad guys. The campy script has the three private eye Angels (Cameron Diaz, Drew Barrymore and Lucy Liu) investigating the theft of two titanium finger rings on which are encrypted the list of people in the federal witness protection program now that several of the witnesses have turned up dead.

But the shallow premise is really just a perfunctory measure on which to drape the exciting action scenes that have Natalie (Diaz), Dylan (Barrymore) and Alex (Liu) scantily clad in haute couture doing flips and kicks (shown in slow motion, of course) to outwit the villains. It's a B.movie with a big budget and name stars that ludicrously equates female empowerment solely with brawn and a bodacious body.

Watching the film, one could understand how young girls could be attracted to the Angels. They are strong, smart, and tough, and they can outkick, outpunch and out.thump their male counterparts while still being feminine and fun. Yet "feminine" has a slightly risque interpretation here, as the women in their skintight (and baring) outfits use not only their flowing hair and bright.white smiles, but their abundant cleavage and tight abs and butts to distract and then clobber the enemy.

However, the film's tone is light.hearted and frivolous, never taking itself, or its actors, too seriously. And the leading ladies join in on the fun, almost winking at the camera as they shake their booties, seeming not to mind the gratuitous shots of the derrieres.

In a tongue.in.cheek homage to "The Matrix," "Mission: Impossible" and the James Bond films, among other well.known (and male.dominated) actioners, "Charlie's Angels: Full Throttle" has the cherub trio performing death.defying feats all in the line of duty. In fact, much like the original "Angels" film, the sequel opens with a 007.like sequence where the Angels make their escape by leaping out of a military truck that has plunged over a bridge and jumping inside an airplane to land safely with their rescued victim. And the action skyrockets from there to include a
dangerous dirt bike race, an over.the.top car chase and many leaps from tall buildings, which of course leave the gorgeous gumshoes relatively unscathed.

Replacing Bill Murray as the new Bosley is Bernie Mac, who adds a bit of zing and his unique comedic flair to the film and acts as a foil to the girls' flirty spy games. John Forsyth returns as the voice of Charlie (still communicating through speaker box), which anchors the film and recalls its TV roots. And in a much.hyped role, Demi Moore stars as Madison Lee, a fallen Angel who just may pose the biggest threat to the good.hearted, crime.fighting threesome. And, as if to justify the apparent millions of dollars supposedly spent on "touching up" her body, the film boasts a few gratuitous shots of Moore running on the beach, "Baywatch".style, or lounging in lacy lingerie and spiked heels as she plots world domination.

The cast seems up for the silly melodramatic style of the film, which has a toe.tapping, finger.snapping score that dares anyone not to bounce along with the beat. Diaz shines as the flighty Natalie, mixing an irrepressible smile and giggle with a deadly "hi.yah!" martial arts chop to thwart the baddies. Liu is still the aloof acrobat, stretching her folded body out of a crate and flipping her hair as if to say, "no big deal." Barrymore keeps up with her buddies, as the former bad.girl.turned.Angel who still has a soft spot for the bad guys.

Goofy, exciting and completely forgettable, "Charlie's Angels: Full Throttle" perfectly fits the definition of popcorn summer fare.

Because of intermittent stylized violence, fleeting crass language and profanity, a live.in relationship and some mild sexual innuendo, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A.III .. adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG.13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
